title: Characters and Conflict
bigQuestion: How does a writer make a made-up person feel so real that you argue about what they should have done?

story.title: The Boy Outside the Theater
story.kicker: A novel written by a teenager opens with one boy, one sidewalk, and a feeling every reader knows.
paragraphs: The book opens with a boy stepping out of a movie theater into bright sunlight. He is alone, and he is thinking about two things: the actor Paul Newman, and how to get home. He has a long walk ahead of him, and he knows that a boy like him, walking alone in his part of town, might get jumped. He walks anyway. Within a few pages he is on the ground with a knife at his throat, and his older brothers are running to pull the attackers off.

The boy is Ponyboy Curtis, fourteen years old, the narrator of The Outsiders. The author, S. E. Hinton, started the novel when she was a high school student in Oklahoma and published it in 1967. She was tired of books about teenagers that did not sound like anyone she knew. So she wrote about the two groups at her own school: the greasers, poor kids with long, oiled hair, and the Socs, rich kids with nice cars. In her book, the greasers tell the story.

What makes that first scene work is not the fight. It is everything Ponyboy tells you before the fight. He says he likes movies and books, which most of his friends do not. He says his oldest brother, Darry, is hard on him. He says he wishes he looked tougher than he does. By the time the Socs pull up, you already know him. You are scared for him because you know him.

That is the trick of every good novel. A writer cannot hand you a real person. A writer can only hand you words: what a character says, does, wants, fears, and notices. From those words you build a person in your head. And once you have built him, you cannot help caring what happens to him. You will argue with friends about whether Darry loves Ponyboy or just bosses him. You will decide who is to blame for what happens in the park.

This chapter is about how that building happens. You will learn how writers show character, what pushes a character to act, how a person can change across three hundred pages, and who gets to tell the story. The Outsiders is the novel this site has its own room for, so it will come up often. But the tools work on any book with a person in it, which is nearly all of them.
story.think: Think of a character from a book, movie, or show you felt you knew. What did the writer show you first that made you care?

lessons.title: Telling and Showing
lessons.mainIdea: Writers reveal character two ways: by telling you directly, or by showing actions, words, looks and thoughts and letting you decide.
reading: Read these two sentences about the same girl. One: Maya was generous. Two: Maya slid half her sandwich across the table without looking up, as if she had never wanted the whole thing. The first sentence tells you what to think. The second makes you figure it out. Both are ways of building a character, and good writers use both.

When the narrator states a trait outright, that is *direct characterization*. It is fast and clear: "Darry was tough, cool, and smart." You do not have to guess. Writers use it when they need you to know something quickly, or when a narrator is the kind of person who sums people up.

When you have to infer a trait from evidence, that is *indirect characterization*. The evidence comes in five kinds: what the character says, what the character does, what the character thinks, how the character looks, and how other people react to the character. Maya sliding the sandwich is an action. Her not looking up is a small action that shows she does not want thanks.

Indirect characterization asks more of you, but it pays more back. When you work out that Maya is generous, you believe it, because you saw the proof. When a book tells you a character is brave and then never shows it, you stop trusting the book. Watch for the gap between what a narrator says about a person and what that person actually does.

words.d: when the narrator or another character states a trait outright, such as "he was stubborn"
when the reader infers a trait from a character's speech, actions, thoughts, looks, or how others treat them
a quality of a person's character, such as honesty, impatience, or courage

look.title: One Sentence, Two Methods
look.text: Mr. Ortiz was the most patient man on the block. He had explained the same bus schedule to Mrs. Kim four times that week, and on the fifth time he only smiled and pulled out a pencil.
look.prompt: Which sentence is direct characterization and which is indirect? Which one would convince you more if it stood alone?

check.q: Which of these is direct characterization?
choices: Lena had a quick temper.
Lena slammed the door so hard the picture fell.
Everyone stepped back when Lena walked in.
Lena's jaw was tight and her fists were closed.
check.why: Only the second sentence states the trait outright. The others give evidence and let you infer it.

check.q: Which of the five kinds of indirect evidence is 'other people stepped back when she walked in'?
choices: What the character says
What the character thinks
How others react to the character
How the character looks
check.why: The evidence is other people's reaction, one of the five kinds of indirect characterization.

check.q: Why can indirect characterization be more convincing than direct?
choices: It uses fewer words
The reader sees the proof and draws the conclusion
It is always more accurate
Narrators are not allowed to state traits
check.why: When readers reach a conclusion from evidence, they believe it more than when they are simply told.

lessons.title: What a Character Wants
lessons.mainIdea: Motivation is the reason behind a character's actions, and finding it explains choices that look strange from outside.
reading: A boy in a novel steals a loaf of bread. Is he a thief? Then you read that his sister has not eaten in two days. Now the same act means something different. Nothing about the action changed. What changed is that you learned his *motivation*, the reason behind what he did.

Every character who matters wants something. It can be big, like freedom or revenge, or small, like being left alone for one afternoon. Writers rarely announce it. They let you see the character reach for it again and again. Ponyboy in The Outsiders wants to be seen as more than a greaser. That want explains why he keeps reading books and watching sunsets, even when his friends tease him.

To find motivation, ask two questions about any action: what does this character get from doing it, and what would they lose by not doing it? A character who lies to a friend might be protecting himself, protecting the friend, or protecting a secret. Each answer makes a different person.

Motivation is also where real conflict starts. Two characters who want different things will collide. Two characters who want the same thing, like one job or one parent's approval, will collide harder. When you can name what each person wants, the whole plot starts to make sense.

words.d: the reason a character does what they do, whether stated or hidden
to work out something not stated directly, using clues and what you already know

look.title: The Same Act, Three Reasons
look.text: Devon volunteers to stay after school and clean the art room every Friday. His teacher thinks he loves art. His best friend thinks he is avoiding the bus. His mother thinks he is hiding from his chores. Only one of them is right, and Devon is not saying.
look.prompt: What clue in a later chapter would prove each explanation right or wrong? Which clue would you look for first?

check.q: What is a character's motivation?
choices: The trait the narrator states most often
What the character looks like
The reason behind what the character does
The problem the character faces at the end
check.why: Motivation is the why behind an action, the want or fear that drives it.

check.q: Learning that the boy's sister was hungry changed what about the bread scene?
choices: What the boy did
Where the scene took place
Who told the story
What the action meant
check.why: The action was the same. The motivation changed how readers understand it.

check.q: Which situation would most likely create the strongest conflict?
choices: Two characters who want different things in different towns
Two characters who want nothing in particular
One character who gets everything easily
Two characters who want the same single thing
check.why: When two people want the same one thing, only one can have it, so they collide hardest.

lessons.title: Hearing Character in Dialogue
lessons.mainIdea: How a character talks, including word choice, what they avoid saying, and how they treat others, reveals who they are.
reading: Two brothers answer the same question: "Where were you?" The first says, "Out." The second says, "I went by the library, then I stopped at Marco's, and then I lost track of time, I'm sorry." You have never met these brothers. You already know that one is closed and one is open, one is maybe angry and one is anxious to be forgiven. Dialogue did that in twenty words.

*Dialogue* is the words characters speak. Writers use it to reveal character in several ways. Word choice shows education, region, and mood. Length shows whether a person is guarded or eager. What a character refuses to talk about can matter more than what they say. And how a character speaks to different people, gently to a child and sharply to a waiter, shows their values.

In The Outsiders, the greasers' slang marks them as a group, and it separates them from the Socs. But within the group, each boy sounds different. Two-Bit jokes constantly. Johnny says little, and when he speaks, the others listen. Ponyboy notices that Cherry Valance, a Soc, talks to him like a person, and that small thing changes how he sees her whole side of town.

When you read dialogue, do not just ask what was said. Ask what the speaker wanted from saying it. Ask what they left out. Ask whether their words match their actions, because a character who says "I don't care" and then checks the window every five minutes has told you something true without meaning to.

words.d: the words characters speak to each other in a story, usually shown in quotation marks
informal words used by a particular group, such as teenagers or a neighborhood

look.title: A Kitchen Argument
look.text: "You didn't call." "Phone died." "It's been dead a lot lately." "Yeah, well." Ray put the milk back in the fridge without drinking any. "Did you eat?" "I said I'm fine." Nobody had asked if he was fine.
look.prompt: What does each speaker want? What does the last line tell you about Ray that he did not intend to say?

check.q: In the brothers' example, what showed that the second brother was anxious to be forgiven?
choices: He spoke in slang
He gave a long, detailed answer ending in an apology
He refused to answer
He spoke to a waiter sharply
check.why: The long, over-explained answer with an apology at the end shows eagerness to be forgiven.

check.q: A character says "I don't care" and then checks the window every five minutes. What should a reader conclude?
choices: The character's actions reveal the words are not true
The character is telling the truth
The window is broken
The narrator is lying
check.why: When words and actions disagree, the actions usually reveal the truth.

check.q: Which question is the most useful one to ask about a line of dialogue?
choices: How many words does it have?
Is it in quotation marks?
What did the speaker want from saying it?
Who is the author?
check.why: Asking what the speaker wanted uncovers motivation and character behind the words.

lessons.title: Static and Dynamic Characters
lessons.mainIdea: A dynamic character changes inside during the story; a static character stays the same, and both kinds have jobs to do.
reading: At the start of a story a girl believes her older cousin is perfect. By the end she has watched him lie, cover it up, and lie again, and she cannot see him the same way. She has not grown taller or changed schools. She has changed inside. A character who changes in some important way is called *dynamic*.

A character who stays the same all through the story is *static*. Static is not an insult. A story needs people who hold steady. A best friend who is loyal on page one and loyal on the last page gives the main character something to lean on. A villain who never softens gives the hero something to push against. The question is not whether a character is good or bad but whether they change.

The change in a dynamic character is usually in beliefs, values, or understanding, not in situation. A character who gets rich but thinks exactly as before is static. A character who loses everything and learns what mattered is dynamic. In The Outsiders, Ponyboy begins by seeing Socs as one thing and greasers as another. By the end he understands that people on both sides watch the same sunset. That is his change.

To track a change, find three moments: how the character sees things at the start, the event that shakes that view, and how they see things at the end. If you can name all three with evidence from the text, you can prove a character is dynamic. If the third moment matches the first, you have a static character, and you can prove that too.

words.d: a character who changes in an important way, usually in beliefs or understanding, during the story
a character who stays essentially the same from the beginning of the story to the end

look.title: Two Friends, One Summer
look.text: In June, Tasha and Rob both think the new kid, Elias, is stuck up. In July, Tasha gets stuck on a broken bus with Elias for four hours and hears about his family. In August, Tasha invites him over. Rob still calls him stuck up and does not know why Tasha bothers.
look.prompt: Which friend is dynamic and which is static? Name the event that shook the view of the one who changed.

check.q: What makes a character dynamic?
choices: Being the main character
Changing inside in an important way
Doing a lot of action
Being likable
check.why: A dynamic character changes in beliefs, values, or understanding. Action or likability is not the test.

check.q: A character wins the lottery but thinks about the world exactly as before. This character is:
choices: Dynamic, because his situation changed
Dynamic, because he is rich now
Static, because his inner view did not change
Static, because he is a minor character
check.why: The change that counts is inside. A changed situation with an unchanged mind is static.

check.q: Why do stories need static characters?
choices: They give the main character something steady to lean on or push against
They are easier to write
They always turn out to be villains
Readers prefer characters who never change
check.why: Steady characters anchor the story, as loyal friends or unchanging opponents.

lessons.title: Conflict Inside
lessons.mainIdea: Internal conflict is a struggle within one character between two things they want, fear, or believe.
reading: A boy finds a wallet with two hundred dollars in it. Nobody saw him pick it up. His family needs the money. He also knows exactly what his grandmother would say. For the next three pages he does nothing but walk and think, and those are the tensest pages in the book. Nobody is chasing him. The fight is inside.

That is *internal conflict*: a struggle within a single character. It is often written as a person versus themselves. The two sides can be a want against a value, a fear against a duty, or two loyalties that cannot both be kept. The character has to choose, and either choice costs something.

Internal conflict is what makes a character feel real rather than like a game piece. A hero who never doubts is boring. A character who wants to run and also wants to stay, who must decide and cannot, is someone you recognize. In The Outsiders, Johnny wrestles with whether to turn himself in after the park, and Ponyboy wrestles with his anger at Darry against his need for him.

You can spot internal conflict by looking for a character's thoughts that argue with each other, a decision that is put off, or a moment when a character does one thing and then undoes it. When you find one, name the two sides. "He wants the money but he wants to be honest" is a complete description of a conflict.

words.d: a struggle inside one character, such as a want fighting a value or two loyalties that cannot both be kept
a choice between two options where each one has a real cost

look.title: Three Pages of Walking
look.text: He counted it again at the corner. Two hundred and six. He thought about the electric bill on the fridge, the one with the red stamp. Then he thought about his grandmother's face, and he put the wallet in his pocket, and he took it out, and he put it back.
look.prompt: Name the two sides of this boy's conflict. What action shows that he has not decided yet?

check.q: Which of these is an internal conflict?
choices: A girl argues with her coach about playing time
A storm floods a family's basement
A boy wants to quit the team but fears letting his father down
Two friends race for the same bus
check.why: The struggle is inside one person, between a want and a fear. The others involve outside forces or other people.

check.q: Why does internal conflict make a character feel real?
choices: Real people doubt and struggle with choices too
It makes the plot longer
It means the character is the narrator
It removes the need for other characters
check.why: Readers recognize inner struggle from their own lives, so a character who has it seems human.

check.q: Which clue best signals internal conflict in a text?
choices: A description of the weather
A change in setting
A new character arriving
A character doing something and then undoing it
check.why: Doing and undoing an action shows a character caught between two choices.

lessons.title: Conflict Outside
lessons.mainIdea: External conflict is a struggle between a character and something outside them: another person, society, nature, or fate.
reading: A swimmer is caught in a current. A student is called to the principal's office over a rule she thinks is unfair. Two boys in a parking lot square up over a girl. In each case the character is pushing against something outside themselves. That is *external conflict*, and most stories have more than one.

Writers and teachers usually sort external conflicts into a few kinds. Person versus person: two characters want different things. Person versus society: a character pushes against laws, customs, or what everyone expects. Person versus nature: a character fights weather, wilderness, or illness. Some add person versus fate or the supernatural, when the force is beyond human control.

The Outsiders runs on person versus society. The greasers and Socs are not just individuals who dislike each other. They are two groups that the whole town has sorted by money, and the boys inherit the fight whether they want it or not. Ponyboy's fight with the Socs at the movie theater is person versus person on the surface, but the reason those boys are enemies is the society behind them.

Internal and external conflicts usually work together. The outside fight forces the inside choice. A boy attacked in a park has an external conflict, and afterward he has an internal one: run or confess. When you describe a story's conflict, try to name one of each and show how the outside one caused the inside one.

words.d: a struggle between a character and an outside force such as another person, society, or nature
the people of a place taken as a whole, with their laws, customs, and expectations

look.title: Conflicts in One Short Model Story
look.cite: counted for this lesson from a ten-scene model story
look.prompt: This story has ten scenes. Which kind of conflict fills the most scenes? Does that tell you what the story is mostly about, or only what is loudest?

check.q: A character struggles against a rule that everyone in town accepts. Which kind of conflict is this?
choices: Person versus nature
Person versus person
Internal conflict
Person versus society
check.why: The opposing force is the customs and expectations of a whole community, which is society.

check.q: In The Outsiders, why are the fights between greasers and Socs more than person versus person?
choices: Because the boys are all related
Because the whole town has sorted them into groups by money
Because they happen in nature
Because the narrator makes them up
check.why: The groups exist because of the town's social divisions, so the conflict is also person versus society.

check.q: How do external and internal conflicts usually relate?
choices: The outside fight often forces an inside choice
They never appear in the same story
Internal conflicts always come first
External conflicts only happen to villains
check.why: An outside event, like an attack, often creates an inner decision, like whether to confess.

lessons.title: First Person
lessons.mainIdea: In first-person point of view, a character tells the story as "I," so you get their thoughts but only what they know and choose to say.
reading: "I never meant to break the window." Five words in and you already have a voice, a person, and a hint that something is being explained away. The story is told by someone inside it, using I and me and my. That is *first-person point of view*. The teller is called the *narrator*.

First person gets you close. You hear the narrator's private thoughts, feel their fear, and hear the way they talk. Twain's Huckleberry Finn opens with Huck speaking straight to you in his own uneducated, honest voice, and that voice is most of why the book works. The Outsiders is first person too: everything comes through Ponyboy, including his mistakes.

But first person has walls. The narrator can only tell what they saw, heard, or were told. If Ponyboy is not in the room, you are not in the room. And a narrator can be wrong, or biased, or protecting someone. When Ponyboy says Darry does not love him, you have his feeling, not the fact. Later he learns otherwise, and so do you, but only because the book lets him find out.

When you read first person, keep two questions running. What does this narrator know? And what does this narrator want me to think? A narrator's blind spots are part of the story. Sometimes they are the whole point.

words.d: the position from which a story is told: who is telling it and how much they know
the voice that tells a story, which may be a character in it or a voice outside it
a point of view in which a character tells the story using I, me, and my

look.title: Huck Introduces Himself
look.text: You don't know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain't no matter.
look.cite: Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, 1884
look.prompt: What can you tell about Huck from this one sentence: his schooling, his attitude, how he treats the reader?

check.q: Which sentence is written in first person?
choices: She locked the door and waited.
I locked the door and waited.
He wondered whether to lock the door.
The door was locked at nine.
check.why: First person uses I, me, and my. Only the second sentence has the narrator inside the story as I.

check.q: What is a main limit of first-person point of view?
choices: The reader never learns the narrator's thoughts
The narrator must always be honest
It cannot be used in novels
The narrator can only tell what they know or were told
check.why: A first-person narrator is inside the story and cannot report scenes they did not witness.

check.q: Ponyboy says early on that Darry does not love him. How should a careful reader treat this?
choices: As a fact the author confirmed
As a clue about the setting
As the narrator's feeling, which might be wrong
As dialogue from Darry
check.why: A first-person narrator reports feelings and beliefs, and Ponyboy later learns he was mistaken.

lessons.title: Third Person: Limited and Omniscient
lessons.mainIdea: Third-person narrators use he, she and they; a limited narrator stays inside one character's mind, while an omniscient narrator can enter any mind.
reading: "Marisol did not hear the footsteps behind her." No character could say that about herself in the moment. The narrator is standing outside the story, using she and her, and knows something Marisol does not. That is *third-person point of view*. It comes in two main kinds, and the difference is how much the narrator can see.

A *limited* third-person narrator follows one character closely, reporting that person's thoughts and feelings but nobody else's. You see the world over that character's shoulder. It feels almost like first person, but the narrator can add things the character would not say, like "she did not hear the footsteps." Many modern novels use limited third person because it is close and clear at the same time.

An *omniscient* narrator, from a Latin word meaning all-knowing, can enter any character's mind and move from one to another, even in the same scene. Dickens often does this: he can tell you what the rich man thinks and then what the beggar at his gate thinks. Omniscient narration gives a wide view of a whole world, but it keeps you a little farther from any one person.

To tell them apart, count minds. If the narrator only ever reports one character's inner life, it is limited. If it reports two or more, it is omniscient. Then ask why the writer chose that. A mystery often stays limited so you cannot see the culprit's thoughts. A novel about a whole town goes omniscient so you can.

words.d: a point of view in which a narrator outside the story tells it using he, she, and they
third-person narration that reports the thoughts of only one character
all-knowing; third-person narration that can report the thoughts of any character

look.title: Counting Minds
look.text: Nia thought the coach had forgotten her name. The coach, watching from the bench, was thinking that Nia was the only player who never gave up, and wondering how to say so without embarrassing her.
look.prompt: How many minds does this narrator enter? Is it limited or omniscient? What do you know that Nia does not?

check.q: A narrator reports only Jamal's thoughts throughout the book, using he and him. This point of view is:
choices: First person
Third-person limited
Third-person omniscient
Second person
check.why: He and him make it third person, and staying inside one mind makes it limited.

check.q: What does omniscient mean?
choices: Telling the story in the past
Using only dialogue
Following one character
All-knowing
check.why: Omniscient comes from Latin words meaning all-knowing. The narrator can enter any mind.

check.q: Why might a mystery writer choose third-person limited?
choices: So the reader cannot see the culprit's thoughts
Because it is required for mysteries
So every character's thoughts are visible
Because it uses the word I
check.why: Staying inside one mind keeps the culprit's thoughts hidden and preserves the mystery.

lessons.title: Narrators You Cannot Trust
lessons.mainIdea: An unreliable narrator tells the story in a way the reader should doubt, and the clues to that doubt are part of the story's meaning.
reading: A narrator opens by insisting he is not mad. He says his senses are sharp, that he heard things in heaven and hell, and that he will tell the story calmly to prove it. Then he explains, very calmly, how he planned a murder for a week. This is Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart," and the more the narrator insists on his sanity, the less you believe him. He is an *unreliable narrator*.

An unreliable narrator is one whose telling you cannot fully trust. Sometimes the narrator lies. More often the narrator is honest but limited: a child who does not understand what the adults are doing, a person so angry they cannot see straight, someone who wants badly to look good. The story is still true in the world of the book. The telling of it is bent.

Writers plant clues so that you can see around the narrator. Look for a gap between what the narrator claims and what other characters do or say. Look for a narrator who protests too much, like Poe's. Look for details the narrator drops without noticing what they mean. Ponyboy is mostly reliable, but he is fourteen and hurt, and when he calls Darry cold, the text shows Darry working two jobs to keep the family together.

Reading an unreliable narrator is like listening to a friend tell a story about a fight they were in. You believe the fight happened. You also know they are the hero of their own version. The skill is to hold both things at once and to keep looking for evidence.

words.d: a narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt, because of lies, limits, or bias
a leaning for or against something that shapes how a person sees and reports it

look.title: Protesting Too Much
look.text: True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?
look.prompt: The narrator has not yet told you what he did. What makes you distrust him already, in just this first sentence?

check.q: What is an unreliable narrator?
choices: A narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt
A narrator who uses third person
A narrator who never appears in the story
A narrator who tells the story out of order
check.why: Unreliable means the reader should not fully trust the telling, because of lies, limits, or bias.

check.q: Which clue most suggests a narrator is unreliable?
choices: The narrator describes the weather
The narrator uses long sentences
The story is set in the past
Other characters' actions contradict what the narrator claims
check.why: A gap between the narrator's claims and what others do is a classic sign of unreliability.

check.q: Why does Poe's narrator insisting he is not mad make readers doubt him?
choices: Because sane people rarely need to insist on it so hard
Because he speaks in third person
Because he admits to lying
Because the story is a comedy
check.why: Protesting too much draws attention to the very thing he denies, so readers grow suspicious.

lessons.title: Inference With Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: An inference about a character is a claim; to make it count, cite the exact words from the text that support it and explain the link.
reading: A student says, "Darry is really scared of losing his brothers." Her teacher asks, "Where?" That one word is the whole skill. In literature, what you think about a character is an *inference*, a conclusion drawn from clues. Inferences are welcome, but they have to be backed by *textual evidence*: words from the book that you can point to.

The strongest evidence is specific. "Darry acts worried" is weak. "Darry yells at Ponyboy for coming home late, then the book shows him working two jobs and turning down college" is strong, because anyone can check it. When you quote, quote only the part that matters, and put it in quotation marks. When you paraphrase, say where it comes from.

Then explain the link. Evidence does not speak for itself. Write the bridge: "Darry yells about a late night because he is responsible for keeping the family together, and one mistake could get his brothers taken away." Now a reader sees the claim, the proof, and the reasoning that connects them.

Good evidence can also prove you wrong, and that is useful. If you think a character is cruel and then find three scenes where he is kind to a stranger, your inference needs to change. Readers who go back to the text with an open mind end up knowing characters better than readers who decide early and stop looking.

words.d: a conclusion drawn from clues in the text combined with what the reader already knows
specific words or details from the text, quoted or paraphrased, that support a claim
a statement you believe is true and are prepared to support with evidence

look.title: Claim, Evidence, Link
look.text: Claim: Mr. Alvarez, the janitor in the model story, is proud of his work. Evidence: he arrives an hour before anyone else, and the narrator notices his name written neatly on every mop handle. Link: people who sign their tools care about them the way an artist cares about a painting.
look.prompt: Is the link convincing? What other evidence from a story would make the claim stronger, and what evidence would weaken it?

check.q: What is textual evidence?
choices: Your opinion about a character
Specific words or details from the text that support a claim
The title of the book
What a friend said about the book
check.why: Textual evidence is drawn from the text itself, quoted or paraphrased, so others can check it.

check.q: Which piece of evidence is strongest for the claim 'Darry is scared of losing his brothers'?
choices: Darry seems worried sometimes
Darry is the oldest brother
Darry works two jobs and yells when Ponyboy comes home late
Darry is tall
check.why: Specific actions that anyone can check in the book make the strongest evidence.

check.q: After the evidence, what must a writer still add?
choices: A second title
More characters
A summary of the whole plot
The explanation linking the evidence to the claim
check.why: Evidence does not speak for itself. The reasoning that connects it to the claim completes the argument.

lessons.title: Following One Character Through a Book
lessons.mainIdea: To understand a character in a whole novel, track them at the start, at turning points, and at the end, and compare the evidence.
reading: A single scene shows you a character in one light. A whole novel shows you the same person under many lights, and the changes between them are where the meaning lives. Reading a whole book well means keeping a record, because by chapter ten you will have forgotten the exact words of chapter one.

One simple method: keep a page for each major character with three columns, labeled start, turning points, and end. Under start, write what the character wants and believes in the first chapters, with page numbers. Under turning points, note each event that pushes on those wants and beliefs. Under end, write what the character wants and believes at the close. Then compare the first and last columns.

Try it with Ponyboy in The Outsiders. At the start he believes the Socs have it easy and Darry is against him. Turning points pile up: a conversation with Cherry about sunsets, the night in the park, the days hiding in the church, the fire, the hospital, the rumble, and a note left in a book. At the end he understands that Socs have troubles too, that Darry was protecting him, and that he can tell this story instead of fighting it.

The last pages of the novel reveal that the whole book is a school assignment Ponyboy has written, and its first line is the same as the line he chooses to begin with. That structure is the author's way of saying the change is real: the boy who walked out of the theater alone is now a writer telling you why. A character sheet lets you prove that with evidence, chapter by chapter.

words.d: an event in a story that changes a character's situation, choices, or understanding
the path of change a character follows from the beginning of a story to the end

look.title: Two Brothers, Words per Line
look.cite: counted for this lesson from a short model story written for it
look.prompt: In this model story, the older brother's lines get longer and the younger brother's get shorter. What change in each character might those numbers show?

check.q: Why keep a written record of a character while reading a novel?
choices: Because tests require it
Because readers forget the exact details of early chapters by the end
Because characters in novels never change
Because it replaces reading the book
check.why: Over hundreds of pages, memory fades. A record lets you compare early and late evidence.

check.q: What does the ending of The Outsiders reveal about the whole book?
choices: It was a dream
It was written by Darry
It is Ponyboy's school assignment, beginning where the book began
It takes place in Chicago
check.why: The last pages show Ponyboy writing the story for a class, starting with the book's own first line.

check.q: On a three-column character sheet, what belongs under turning points?
choices: Events that push on the character's wants and beliefs
The character's name and age
The book's chapter titles
The reader's favorite quotes
check.why: Turning points are the events that change a character's situation or understanding.

review.q: 'Rosa never once looked at the clock during the three-hour exam.' This is an example of:
choices: Indirect characterization through action
Direct characterization
Omniscient narration
External conflict
review.why: The sentence shows an action and lets the reader infer focus or calm. Nothing is stated outright.

review.q: A character who is loyal at the start and equally loyal at the end is best described as:
choices: Unreliable
Dynamic
Static
Omniscient
review.why: A character who does not change inside is static, whether or not the character is admirable.

review.q: Which is an example of internal conflict?
choices: A hiker lost in a blizzard
A boy who wants to tell the truth but fears losing his friend
Two sisters fighting over one bedroom
A worker who protests an unfair law
review.why: The struggle is inside one person, between a want and a fear.

review.q: In The Outsiders, the conflict between greasers and Socs is mainly:
choices: Person versus nature
Internal conflict
Person versus fate
Person versus society
review.why: The groups are made by the town's divisions of money and class, so the conflict is social.

review.q: A narrator uses 'she' and reports the thoughts of every character in the room. This is:
choices: Third-person omniscient
Third-person limited
First person
Unreliable narration
review.why: Third person with access to all minds is omniscient.

review.q: What is the best sign that a narrator is unreliable?
choices: The narrator uses first person
The narrator is a teenager
What other characters do contradicts what the narrator claims
The story has a sad ending
review.why: A gap between the narrator's claims and the evidence in the text signals unreliability.

review.q: Which is the strongest textual evidence that a character is generous?
choices: The narrator says she seems nice
She gives her only coat to a stranger on page 42
She is the main character
The reader likes her
review.why: A specific, checkable action from the text is the strongest evidence.

review.q: What is the main reason to track a character across a whole novel instead of judging from one scene?
choices: Because one scene shows one light and the changes between scenes carry the meaning
Because novels have more pages
Because characters are always dynamic
Because tests ask about chapter one
review.why: Change over the whole book is where a character's arc and the story's meaning appear.
